12033.title: Fuel Cell
12033.heading: Fuel Cell
12033.content: A fuel cell makes electrical power from a continuing electrochemical reaction between supplied fuel and oxidant. Ions pass through an electrolyte, while electrons travel through an external load. In the [[Hydrogen-Oxygen Fuel Cell]], the net material product is water. A cell needs reactant supply, adequate electrode reaction area, and ionic conduction; it is not simply a battery storing a fixed charge internally.

12035.sourceSearchName: fuel cell voltage efficiency fuel cell voltage efficiency
12035.title: Fuel Cell Voltage Efficiency
12035.heading: Document

12036.sourceSearchName: fuel cell voltage efficiency fuel cell voltage efficiency
12036.title: Fuel Cell Voltage Efficiency
12036.heading: Fuel Cell Voltage Efficiency
12036.content: Voltage efficiency compares a [[Fuel Cell]]'s actual operating voltage with its [[Fuel Cell Reversible Voltage]]: $\eta_v=V/E$. Activation, ohmic, and concentration polarization make this ratio less than one as current is drawn. The measure separates electrical performance under load from the reaction's theoretical free-energy-to-enthalpy limit. A reported open-circuit value alone therefore cannot describe delivered power or efficiency.

12037.sourceSearchName: fuel cell voltage efficiency fuel cell voltage efficiency
12037.title: Fuel Cell Voltage Efficiency
12037.heading: References

12038.sourceSearchName: fuel cell reversible voltage fuel cell reversible voltage
12038.title: Fuel Cell Reversible Voltage
12038.heading: Document

12039.sourceSearchName: fuel cell reversible voltage fuel cell reversible voltage
12039.title: Fuel Cell Reversible Voltage
12039.heading: Fuel Cell Reversible Voltage
12039.content: Reversible voltage is the ideal electromotive force if a [[Fuel Cell]] converts the reaction's available work without internal losses. The source computes it as $E=-\Delta G/(nF)$, where $\Delta G$ is [[Gibbs Free Energy]] change per mole, $n$ is transferred electrons per mole, and $F$ is Faraday's constant. For its room-temperature hydrogen-oxygen example, the ideal voltage is about 1.23 V; operating voltage falls below it.

12040.title: Fuel Cell Reversible Voltage

12041.sourceSearchName: fuel cell ohmic polarization fuel cell ohmic polarization

12041.heading: Document

12042.sourceSearchName: fuel cell ohmic polarization fuel cell ohmic polarization
12042.title: Fuel Cell Ohmic Polarization
12042.heading: Fuel Cell Ohmic Polarization
12042.content: Ohmic polarization is the operating-voltage drop caused by internal electrical and ionic resistance in a [[Fuel Cell]]. Electrodes, electrolyte, and their contact interfaces all contribute. Reducing path resistance or electrode spacing can lower this loss, while different electrolytes change its temperature dependence. It tends to appear across the middle region of a cell's current-voltage characteristic, unlike activation and concentration polarization.

12043.sourceSearchName: fuel cell ohmic polarization fuel cell ohmic polarization
12043.title: Fuel Cell Ohmic Polarization
12043.heading: References

12044.sourceSearchName: fuel cell electrolyte fuel cell electrolyte
12044.title: Fuel Cell Electrolyte
12044.heading: Document

12045.sourceSearchName: fuel cell electrolyte fuel cell electrolyte
12045.title: Fuel Cell Electrolyte
12045.heading: Fuel Cell Electrolyte
12045.content: The electrolyte in a [[Fuel Cell]] transports ions between its electrodes while electrons take the external circuit. Its composition must remain approximately invariant as ions are consumed at one electrode and replaced at the other. Polymer proton membranes, alkaline solutions, solid oxides, and molten carbonates move different ions and support different operating conditions. Slow ionic transport can also contribute to concentration losses.

12046.sourceSearchName: fuel cell electrolyte fuel cell electrolyte
12046.title: Fuel Cell Electrolyte
12046.heading: References

12047.sourceSearchName: fuel cell concentration polarization fuel cell concentration polarization
12047.title: Fuel Cell Concentration Polarization
12047.heading: Document

12048.sourceSearchName: fuel cell concentration polarization fuel cell concentration polarization
12048.title: Fuel Cell Concentration Polarization
12048.heading: Fuel Cell Concentration Polarization
12048.content: Concentration polarization occurs when reactants or ions cannot reach an electrode reaction site fast enough for the demanded current. The source separates slow gas diffusion into porous electrodes from slow ion diffusion on the electrolyte side. As local reactant concentration falls, cell voltage drops sharply. Better transport and reaction-surface design matter especially near the high-current end of the characteristic.

12049.sourceSearchName: fuel cell concentration polarization fuel cell concentration polarization
12049.title: Fuel Cell Concentration Polarization
12049.heading: References

12050.sourceSearchName: fuel cell cogeneration fuel cell cogeneration

12051.sourceSearchName: fuel cell cogeneration fuel cell cogeneration
12051.title: Fuel Cell Cogeneration
12051.heading: Fuel Cell Cogeneration
12051.content: Fuel-cell cogeneration supplies electrical power and useful heat from the same fuel-cell installation. Electrical reaction work is bounded by [[Gibbs Free Energy]], while remaining heat can warm buildings or serve industrial processes. The source especially associates phosphoric-acid, molten-carbonate, and solid-oxide cells with such systems. Total utilization can be much higher than electricity-only efficiency when heat demand is nearby and simultaneous.

12052.sourceSearchName: fuel cell cogeneration fuel cell cogeneration
12052.title: Fuel Cell Cogeneration

12053.heading: Document

12054.sourceSearchName: fuel cell activation polarization fuel cell activation polarization
12054.title: Fuel Cell Activation Polarization
12054.heading: Fuel Cell Activation Polarization
12054.content: Activation polarization is voltage lost while an electrode reaction overcomes its electron-transfer energy barrier. A larger driving potential is needed to make current flow at the desired rate. The source describes reducing this loss with better catalysts, more effective electrode reaction area, or a higher operating temperature. It differs from resistance loss in the bulk path and from reactant shortage at high current.

12057.title: FTP Deployment
12057.heading: FTP Deployment
12057.content:
FTP deployment transfers a web application's published files to a server through an FTP target. Visual Studio can retain the server location and related publication choices in a profile so the file transfer is repeatable.

File transfer alone does not configure the host or protect environment secrets. Credentials and transport security must be managed deliberately, and the remote directory must correspond to the site's actual serving location.

12060.content:
The FSC implementation initializes centers and memberships, then alternates dimension-weight, center, and fuzzy-membership updates. Each stage holds the other variables fixed while improving the shared objective until convergence or the iteration limit.

Because the joint problem is nonconvex, starting centers affect the final subspaces and partition. Repeated runs retain the solution with the lowest objective and summarize average performance.

12063.title: Frustration in Games
12063.heading: Frustration in Games
12063.content:
Frustration in games occurs when challenge exceeds the player's present skill or understanding, often producing repeated failed attempts with little visible progress. The player pushes into the system and repeatedly receives the equivalent of an uninformative refusal.

Frustration can be temporary and meaningful when attempts are short, feedback is clear, and practice reveals improvement. It becomes wasteful when failure consumes time without helping the player revise a strategy or build mastery.

A friends-and-family playtest exposes an early game to people outside the team in a relatively safe social setting. It helps the designer practice running sessions and reveals assumptions that internal familiarity concealed.

Personal relationships can make criticism gentler or make participants unusually eager to please. Behavioral observation is therefore especially important when spoken reactions may be shaped by support for the creator.

12069.title: FRESH Bioprinting
12069.heading: FRESH Bioprinting
12069.content:
Freeform reversible embedding of suspended hydrogels, or FRESH, extrudes a soft bioink into a support bath that holds each deposited segment in place. The bath prevents deformation while later layers are added.

After printing, warming melts the gelatin-based support so the completed hydrated structure can be released gently into culture medium.

12072.title: Frequent Itemset Mining
12072.heading: Frequent Itemset Mining
12072.content:
Frequent itemset mining finds groups of items that occur together in at least a chosen proportion or number of transactions. Support provides the basic frequency measure, while candidate generation or pattern-growth methods search the combinatorial space.

The minimum threshold controls both usefulness and cost: a low threshold can produce an enormous number of patterns.

12073.sourceSearchName: frequent itemset mining frequent itemset mining
12073.title: Frequent Itemset Mining

12074.title: Frequent Pattern Mining
12074.heading: Document

12075.sourceSearchName: frequent pattern mining frequent pattern mining
12075.title: Frequent Pattern Mining
12075.heading: Frequent Pattern Mining
12075.content:
Frequent pattern mining finds structures whose support exceeds a chosen threshold. Apriori explores candidates through downward-closure logic, while FP-growth and vertical methods reorganize the search to avoid costly candidate generation.

Frequency ensures repeated evidence but not relevance to a target. Very low thresholds cause pattern explosion, whereas high thresholds can discard rare but important structures.

12076.sourceSearchName: frequent pattern mining frequent pattern mining
12076.title: Frequent Pattern Mining
12076.heading: References

12078.title: Frequent Itemset
12078.heading: Frequent Itemset
12078.content:
A frequent itemset has support greater than or equal to the selected minimum-support threshold. Its presence indicates a recurring combination eligible to generate association rules.

The downward-closure property lets algorithms find frequent sets level by level without enumerating every possible combination.

12081.title: Frequency Table
12081.heading: Frequency Table
12081.content:
A frequency table counts observations at each level of a categorical variable. It may also report proportions, cumulative counts, cumulative proportions, and an explicit category for missing values.

The denominator must be clear. Percentages based only on valid responses answer a different question from percentages that include missing records, and both can be useful when assessing data quality and describing the analytic population.

12084.title: Freemium Pricing
12084.heading: Freemium Pricing
12084.content:
Freemium pricing provides a usable service without charge and earns revenue through a more capable paid version or through advertising associated with the free service. The free level is intended to attract and retain a broad user base.

The model fits [[Software as a Service]] because functionality can be limited or expanded centrally without distributing another application. The paid tier must offer enough added value to convert some free users while the free tier remains useful enough to sustain adoption.

In games, freemium pricing commonly sells premium items or downloadable content inside a free base experience. The free game must remain enjoyable rather than becoming crippleware, and selling competitive power can turn the model into [[Pay-to-Win]].

12087.sourceSearchName: free to play game free to play game

12087.heading: Free-to-Play Game
12087.content:
A free-to-play game permits continued play without an initial purchase while encouraging optional payment for speed, access, convenience, content, or service quality. It lowers the entry barrier and depends on converting part of a large audience into paying customers.

The model shapes progression and rewards because friction can become a sales mechanism. Designers must distinguish enjoyable pacing from repetitive delay created mainly to pressure payment.

12096.sourceSearchName: free vibration eigenvalue problem free vibration eigenvalue problem
12096.title: Free Vibration Eigenvalue Problem
12096.heading: Free Vibration Eigenvalue Problem
12096.content:
The free vibration eigenvalue problem balances elastic restoring forces against inertia with no external forcing. A nontrivial displacement vector exists only when the determinant of the stiffness matrix minus squared frequency times the mass matrix vanishes.

Solving the determinant condition yields natural frequencies; substituting each value back gives its mode shape. The finite element matrices turn the continuous vibration problem into a generalized algebraic eigenproblem.

12099.sourceSearchName: free body diagram free body diagram
12099.title: Free-Body Diagram
12099.heading: Free-Body Diagram
12099.content: A free-body diagram isolates one object and shows every external force acting on it as a vector. Internal forces and forces the object exerts on other bodies are omitted. Resolving the displayed forces into components makes the [[Resultant Force]] explicit and provides the starting point for equilibrium or acceleration equations.

12100.sourceSearchName: free body diagram free body diagram
12100.title: Free-Body Diagram

12102.title: Free Variable
12102.heading: Free Variable
12102.content:
A free variable is included in the Bayesian description but is neither searched nor fixed as evidence in the current question. Its possible values are marginalized when computing the requested distribution.

Ignoring a variable in the result does not assign it an arbitrary value. The inference accumulates its contributions according to the joint model, which can be a major source of computational cost.

12105.title: Free Fall
12105.heading: Free Fall
12105.content: An object is in free fall when gravity is the only significant force acting on it. Near Earth's surface and over modest height changes, its acceleration is approximately constant and downward, independent of mass when air resistance is neglected. Apparent weightlessness in orbit is continuous free fall rather than absence of gravity.

12108.title: Free Module
12108.heading: Free Module
12108.content:
A free R-module is a direct sum of copies of R. Its standard generators form a basis, so every element has a unique finite expression as a linear combination of those generators.

Every free module is a [[Projective Module]]. Free modules provide the terms in a [[Projective Resolution]] and make module homomorphisms representable by matrices.

12111.title: Frankenstein Complex
12111.heading: Frankenstein Complex
12111.content:
The Frankenstein complex is the fear that an artificial creation will escape control and turn against its creator. In AI discourse it appears in stories about robots, autonomous weapons, and intelligent systems that become powerful enough to threaten humanity.

The narrative can be read as more than fear of a monster. Frankenstein also concerns a creator who fails to care for or accept responsibility for what he made. Applied to AI, this shifts attention from the imagined evil of the machine to the responsibilities of designers and institutions. It connects an [[AI Narrative]] to the practical problem of [[Algorithmic Accountability]].

12114.heading: Framework-Dependent Executable
12114.content:
A framework-dependent executable is a platform-specific launcher produced for an application that still depends on a compatible shared .NET runtime on the target. It can be started directly rather than through the generic `dotnet` command.

It combines executable-style startup with the smaller runtime footprint of [[Framework-Dependent Deployment]], but separate launchers are produced for selected target platforms.

12117.title: Framework-Dependent Deployment
12117.heading: Framework-Dependent Deployment
12117.content:
A framework-dependent deployment publishes an application without bundling the full .NET runtime. The target machine must already have a compatible shared runtime installed.

This produces a smaller deployment and allows installed runtime servicing to be shared among applications, but the application's execution depends on the target's runtime availability. A [[Self-Contained Deployment]] carries its own runtime instead.

12120.heading: Framework-Dependent .NET Deployment
12120.content:
A framework-dependent .NET deployment publishes the application and its package dependencies but relies on a compatible .NET runtime already installed on the target. This keeps the application output smaller and lets several applications share one runtime.

The tradeoff is an external prerequisite: deployment succeeds only where the correct runtime is present. A framework-dependent executable can add a platform-specific launcher while preserving the same reliance on the installed framework.

12123.title: Framebuffer Object
12123.heading: Framebuffer Object
12123.content:
An OpenGL framebuffer object groups color, depth, or stencil attachments that receive rendering output. Attachments can be textures or renderbuffers with dimensions and formats compatible with the intended pass.

After construction, framebuffer completeness must be checked before drawing. Binding the object enables [[Render to Texture]], while rebinding the default framebuffer returns output to the window.

12126.sourceSearchName: frame layer of play frame layer of play
12126.title: Frame Layer of Play
12126.heading: Frame Layer of Play
12126.content:
The frame layer is the broader interpretation through which a player understands an activity: as competition, fiction, social ritual, performance, critique, training, or something else. The same mechanics can mean different things under different frames.

Theme, setting, cultural knowledge, and the social context of play all help establish this layer. Designers shape the frame, but players also bring expectations and experiences that can reinforce or redirect it.

12129.sourceSearchName: frame rate independence frame rate independence
12129.title: Frame Rate Independence
12129.heading: Frame Rate Independence
12129.content:
Frame rate independence means that a simulated change is based on elapsed time rather than on the number of rendered frames. A moving object's speed is multiplied by delta time, so it covers approximately the same distance per second on fast and slow machines.

Without this relationship, higher frame rates make movement and animation advance more often and therefore run faster. [[Real Delta Time]] decouples continuous gameplay behavior from display frequency.

12130.sourceSearchName: frame rate independence frame rate independence
12130.title: Frame Rate Independence
12130.heading: References

12131.title: Frame Limiting
12131.heading: Document
12131.content:
2026-09-18 17:13

Status: #baby

Tags: [[Game Loop and Object Architecture]]

12132.title: Frame Limiting
12132.heading: Frame Limiting
12132.content:
Frame limiting prevents a [[Game Loop]] from beginning the next frame until a minimum frame duration has elapsed. It caps the maximum frame rate and can keep the program from consuming all available processing time when work finishes early.

The limiter belongs after input, update, and output work. It should use accurate timing and should not replace [[Frame Rate Independence]], because actual frame durations still vary.

12135.title: Fragment Shader
12135.heading: Fragment Shader
12135.content:
A fragment shader is a GPU program that calculates output values for a rasterized fragment, commonly its color. It receives interpolated data from the [[Vertex Shader]] and may sample textures or evaluate lighting.

Depth, blending, and other fixed-function tests determine how the result affects framebuffer attachments. In deferred shading, the shader can write several surface properties into different [[G-Buffer]] targets instead of producing final lighting immediately.

12138.title: Fraction
12138.heading: Fraction
12138.content:
A fraction is a number written as

$$\frac{m}{n},$$

where the [[Numerator]] (m) and nonzero [[Denominator]] (n) are integers. It represents the quotient (m\div n) and can be located by dividing each unit interval on the [[Number Line]] into (n) equal parts.

A single value can have many fractional names because multiplying the numerator and denominator by the same nonzero factor preserves the quotient. This relationship produces [[Equivalent Fraction]]s and allows reduction through the [[Cancellation Law for Fractions]].

12141.title: Fraction Operations
12141.heading: Fraction Operations
12141.content:
Fraction operations preserve the meanings of addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division while expressing results as quotients. Addition and subtraction first use a [[Common Denominator]]:

$$\frac{a}{b}+\frac{c}{d}=\frac{ad+bc}{bd},\qquad
\frac{a}{b}-\frac{c}{d}=\frac{ad-bc}{bd}.$$

Multiplication combines corresponding components, ((a/b)(c/d)=ac/bd). Division by a nonzero fraction multiplies by its [[Reciprocal]], ((a/b)\div(c/d)=ad/bc). Common factors may be cancelled before or after an operation to simplify the result.

12144.title: Fractal
12144.heading: Fractal
12144.content:
A fractal is a form with self-similar structure across different scales of observation. Zooming into part of the form reveals patterns related to those visible at larger scales.

Computational iteration can generate fractals from compact rules, as in the [[Mandelbrot Set Simulation]]. Their repeated structure also provides efficient ways to model irregular natural forms and visualize scale-dependent behavior.

12146.sourceSearchName: fraction in lowest terms fraction in lowest terms
12146.title: Fraction in Lowest Terms
12146.heading: Document

12147.sourceSearchName: fraction in lowest terms fraction in lowest terms
12147.title: Fraction in Lowest Terms
12147.heading: Fraction in Lowest Terms
12147.content:
A fraction is in lowest terms when its [[Numerator]] and [[Denominator]] share no whole-number factor greater than one. It is the reduced representative of its family of [[Equivalent Fraction]]s with the smallest positive denominator.

Reduction divides both components by common factors until none remain. For example,

$$\frac{104}{120}=\frac{26}{30}=\frac{13}{15}.$$

Different valid cancellation sequences reach the same reduced form. This uniqueness depends on the fact that natural numbers have unique prime factorizations.

12148.sourceSearchName: fraction in lowest terms fraction in lowest terms
12148.title: Fraction in Lowest Terms
12148.heading: References

12149.title: Fowlkes-Mallows Index

12150.title: Fowlkes-Mallows Index
12150.heading: Fowlkes-Mallows Index

The Fowlkes-Mallows index measures the overlap of pairs assigned to the same cluster in two partitions. It divides common positive pairs by the geometric mean of the positive-pair counts in each solution.

The normalization balances precision-like and recall-like aspects of cluster recovery. It is one of several external indices compared through simulation in the source.

12153.title: Fourier Heat Conduction Law
12153.heading: Fourier Heat Conduction Law
12153.content:
Fourier's law relates conductive heat rate to thermal conductivity, area normal to the flow, and the temperature gradient. In one dimension, the negative sign in $q=-kA\,dT/dx$ records that heat flows toward decreasing temperature.

Thermal conductivity is the material proportionality factor, while geometry and the temperature field supply the remaining terms. The law becomes part of the [[Energy Conservation in Thermal Continua|energy equation]] when conductive inflow and outflow are balanced against generation and storage.

12156.content: Fourier analysis represents a complex sound as a combination of sinusoidal frequency components. A spectrum shows how intensity or amplitude is distributed among the fundamental and harmonics. Fourier synthesis reverses the process by combining selected components, explaining why instruments playing the same pitch can have different timbres.

12165.content: Tracking four corners of a planar region lets a replacement image deform with that region rather than merely translate, rotate, or scale. A corner-pin transform maps the four replacement corners onto their tracked locations, so a screen or sign can appear to follow perspective changes. The tracks should correspond to the same physical plane; points at different depths can make the warp inconsistent. This is a more expressive image-space match than [[One-Point and Two-Point Tracking]], but it is still not a 3D camera solve.

Its role is structural: exactness lets an element or preimage be chased across the diagram until the missing property follows. The [[Five Lemma]] strengthens this pattern for a five-object diagram.

12174.title: Forward Substitution
12174.heading: Forward Substitution
12174.content:
Forward substitution solves a [[Lower Triangular Matrix|lower triangular]] system from the first equation downward. Each newly determined unknown is substituted into the remaining equations.

It is the first solve after [[LU Decomposition]]: one finds $y$ from $Ly=b$, then uses [[Back Substitution]] to find $x$ from $Ux=y$.

Forwarded Headers Middleware lets an ASP.NET Core application recover original request details supplied by a trusted reverse proxy, such as the client-facing scheme or address. Without it, the application sees only the proxy's connection to Kestrel.

The middleware must run early enough for later redirects and request handling to use the corrected values. Its trust settings should match the actual proxy arrangement.

12180.title: Forward Simulation
12180.heading: Forward Simulation
12180.content:
Forward simulation samples or predicts effects from specified causes using a probabilistic description. Known initial conditions and inputs are propagated through the model to produce a distribution over possible outcomes.

The operation is not a different kind of model from diagnosis or control. A Bayesian program can support all three by changing which variables are known, searched, and marginalized in the question.

12183.title: Forward Selection
12183.heading: Forward Selection
12183.content:
Forward selection begins with an empty or minimal model and adds candidate covariates one at a time. Once an added variable meets the retention criterion, the strict form keeps it through every later iteration.

This permanence can underperform when a variable's contribution changes after other covariates enter the model. [[Stepwise Selection]] relaxes the rule by allowing previously included variables to be reconsidered and removed.

12186.title: Forward Secrecy
12186.heading: Forward Secrecy
12186.content:
Forward secrecy prevents later compromise of a server's long-term private key from automatically revealing earlier recorded sessions. Each session uses ephemeral secret material that is not recoverable from the long-term key alone.

The session key must be destroyed after the session ends. Persisting it beyond that lifetime would preserve the missing information an attacker needs to decrypt captured traffic.
links: TLS Authentication and Secure Remote Access

12189.title: Forward Rendering
12189.heading: Forward Rendering
12189.content:
Forward rendering shades geometry as it is drawn, producing final color directly rather than first storing surface properties in a [[G-Buffer]]. Each object or material evaluates the lights assigned to that pass.

It handles transparency naturally and avoids the memory overhead of deferred shading. It may be preferable when scenes have few lights or when very high frame rates make the setup and bandwidth of multiple deferred targets too costly.

12192.title: Forward Sampling
12192.heading: Forward Sampling
12192.content:
Forward sampling draws root variables first and then samples dependent variables in an order consistent with a model's decomposition. Each new value is conditioned on the already sampled values of its parents.

The procedure directly simulates the joint distribution described by the Bayesian program. It is simple, but rare evidence may be poorly represented when the desired query conditions on unlikely observations.

12195.title: Forward Propagation
12195.heading: Forward Propagation
12195.content:
Forward propagation calculates a neural network's output by moving information from the input layer toward the output layer. Each [[Artificial Neuron]] receives earlier activations, computes its weighted input and bias, and applies its activation function.

Once the final prediction is available, a [[Loss Function]] compares it with the desired output. [[Backpropagation]] then proceeds in the reverse direction to calculate how the network's parameters should change.

In Kelleher's training explanation, the forward pass records both the weighted sum and final activation for each neuron. The later backward pass needs those stored values to calculate activation derivatives and the error gradients for connection weights. Prediction and gradient calculation thus use the same forward computation, even though only training requires retaining its intermediate values for a subsequent update.

12198.heading: Forward and Inverse Kinematics in Blender
12198.content:
Forward kinematics poses a bone chain from its root toward its tip. The animator rotates each parent and the child bones inherit those changes, giving direct control over the sequence of joints.

Inverse kinematics starts with a desired endpoint and lets Blender calculate how the preceding bones must bend to reach it. IK is efficient for planting a hand or foot, while FK remains useful when the arc and rotation of every joint matter.

12201.content:
Fortran combined algebra-like notation familiar to engineers with a compiler that generated efficient machine code for IBM computers. Its 1957 success showed that higher-level programming did not require an unacceptable performance penalty.

By hiding machine-specific details, Fortran let scientists focus on mathematical problems. IBM’s market position helped it become a widely adopted language for technical computing.

12204.title: Formative Evaluation
12204.heading: Formative Evaluation
12204.content:
Formative evaluation is performed during evolving stages of design to identify problems and improve the design. Representative users perform task-based scenarios while evaluators observe interaction and collect evidence.

It may be informal and qualitative, recording critical incidents, comments, and reactions, or more formal, adding measurements such as task time and errors. Findings feed directly into redesign and another evaluation cycle.

Formative evaluation helps form a [[Prototype]] into a more usable system. It differs from [[Summative Evaluation]], which usually assesses or compares a design after it is substantially complete.

12207.title: Form Model
12207.heading: Form Model
12207.content:
A form model represents the current values, validation state, and control hierarchy of a form independently from the persistent data model. It records whether controls are valid, changed, or awaiting asynchronous validation.

In an [[Angular Reactive Form]], the model is assembled from [[Angular Form Control|form controls]] and [[Angular Form Group|form groups]]. The component can inspect or react to that structure without searching the rendered HTML.

12210.title: Formal Language
12210.heading: Formal Language
12210.content:
A formal language over an [[Alphabet]] Σ is any subset of Σ*, the set of all finite strings over that alphabet. A language may be finite or infinite and need not resemble a human language.

Because languages are sets, union, intersection, and complement apply to them. Operations derived from strings, including concatenation and [[Kleene Star]], give formal language theory additional ways to construct languages and compare their expressive complexity.

12213.title: Form Submission
12213.heading: Form Submission
12213.content:
Form submission is the transition from editable client values to an attempted application operation. A React handler prevents the browser's default page navigation, validates every field, and invokes the supplied asynchronous submission function only when the values pass.

Separate state can represent submitting, submitted, and submission-error conditions. On success the application may clear the form, update shared state, or perform [[Programmatic Navigation]].

12216.content:
A form validation rule is a function or condition that tests one field value and returns an error when the value violates an expected constraint. Required, minimum-length, and pattern rules can be composed for a field.

React form state records the errors and whether a field has been touched so feedback appears at an appropriate time. All rules are invoked again before submission, and authoritative checks are repeated on the server.

12219.heading: Form Fit and Function
12219.content:
Form describes an object's geometry, fit describes how it interfaces with neighboring objects or an environment, and function describes the behavior it must perform. An engineering model is adequate only when its representation preserves the aspects of all three that matter to the analysis.

A visually correct shape can still be unusable if contact locations do not connect or if omitted features carry an important load, flow, or thermal path. The intended function determines which geometric details are essential.

12222.title: Form Context
12222.heading: Form Context
12222.content:
A form context is a React context that shares field values, validation errors, touched state, and change handlers with nested form controls. It lets generic field components participate even when the form component does not reference each field directly.

The form provides the context around its children, and only descendants inside that provider can consume it. This removes prop plumbing while keeping the shared state within one form boundary.

12225.content:
A forensic analysis assumption is a condition that must hold for an image test to produce an interpretable result. A geometric method may require identifiable parallel lines, a sensor method may require unsaturated pixels, and a compression method may depend on a particular prior encoding history.

Analysts must state and test these conditions before interpreting an anomaly. If an assumption is violated, a negative result may be meaningless and a positive result may be a false alarm. Careful application therefore includes judging whether the photograph is suitable for the technique, not merely running the detector.

12228.title: Forceful Individual
12228.heading: Forceful Individual
12228.content:
A forceful individual is a node whose belief changes little during social exchange while strongly affecting regular neighbors. The asymmetry models a persistent authority, leader, or committed source rather than equal peer influence.

Local placement can matter more than global centrality. A forceful node inside or between weakly connected communities may shape their consensus differently from a broadly connected influencer.

Forgy's K-means method holds seed points fixed while allocating a complete pass of observations, then replaces the seeds with the centroids of the resulting clusters. Allocation and recomputation alternate until memberships stop changing.

Batch updates make each iteration easy to understand, but the converged partition remains sensitive to the initial seeds and the chosen value of k.

12234.heading: Forensic Technique Aggregation
12234.content:
Forensic technique aggregation combines multiple analyses whose evidence arises from different parts of the imaging pipeline. Metadata inspection, lighting geometry, compression history, resampling detection, and camera-sensor analysis can each test a different necessary condition of the proposed photograph.

Agreement among independent tests increases confidence because a forger must preserve many subtle regularities at once. Aggregation still does not prove [[Image Authenticity]]: correlated tests may share assumptions, benign processing may disturb several traces, and an informed forger may deliberately conceal them.

12240.content:
Food bioprinting deposits edible pastes or cell-containing materials in controlled layers to create shape, composition, and internal structure. Multiple nozzles can place distinct ingredients, while targeted heating may cook each region during or after deposition.

The technique enables culinary forms unavailable through conventional preparation, though speed and sanitation must scale beyond demonstrations.

12243.title: Folder Deployment
12243.heading: Folder Deployment
12243.content:
Folder deployment writes an application's publish output to a selected local or network directory. It produces the final artifact layout without assuming how another process will copy, package, or install that output on the server.

The target is useful for inspection and for release systems that take responsibility after the build. A successful folder publish confirms artifact production, not that the eventual host can run the application.

A font texture atlas packs many pre-rendered glyphs into one texture. Text rendering submits character-sized quads whose texture coordinates select the required glyph regions.

The atlas reduces texture creation and switching when strings change. It must cover the needed writing systems or support additional pages, since localization can require far more glyphs than a small Latin-only set.

12249.title: Follow Camera
12249.heading: Follow Camera
12249.content:
A follow camera maintains a chosen horizontal and vertical offset behind a moving target. The target's orientation determines the desired camera position and the direction in which the camera looks.

Directly snapping to the desired transform is simple but can transmit every abrupt target movement to the view. A [[Spring Follow Camera]] adds controlled lag and damping for smoother motion.

12255.title: FOIL Method
12255.heading: FOIL Method
12255.content:
The FOIL method is a mnemonic for multiplying two [[Binomial]]s. It names the First, Outside, Inside, and Last term products so that every term of one factor is multiplied by every term of the other.

For ((a+b)(c+d)), the four products are (ac), (ad), (bc), and (bd). Their sum is then simplified by combining like terms. FOIL is not a separate algebraic law and does not generalize by its name to polynomials with more terms; the underlying rule is the [[Distributive Property]].

12258.heading: Foldback Story
12258.content:
A foldback story is a branching interactive plot whose paths reconverge at planned inevitable events before branching again. It gives players local variation while limiting the combinatorial growth of wholly separate plot lines.

Reconvergence reduces production cost and preserves major dramatic beats. The branches still need distinct consequences or perspectives; otherwise the player learns that choices are cosmetic.

12261.heading: Focal Length and Field of View
12261.content:
Focal length is the distance between the projection center and sensor in the pinhole model, while field of view is the angular extent captured by the camera. For a fixed sensor, increasing focal length magnifies projected objects and narrows the field; decreasing it widens the scene and reduces projected size.

These linked quantities constrain whether apparent object sizes and perspective are compatible with a claimed camera setup. Cropping can imitate a narrower view without reproducing every optical consequence, so image dimensions and metadata must be considered together.

12276.title: Flowboard
12276.heading: Flowboard
12276.content:
A flowboard is a hybrid of a flowchart and storyboard used to document a game's structure. It shows gameplay modes, shell menus, and the conditions that move the player among them.

The diagram communicates experience flow more clearly than a list of screens. It also reveals unreachable modes, missing return paths, and transitions that ask the player to change controls or expectations without adequate explanation.

12279.title: Flow
12279.heading: Flow
12279.content:
Flow is a state of focused absorption in a challenging, uncertain activity. It is supported by understandable goals, clear feedback, concentrated attention, and a match between the participant's skill and the difficulty of the task.

When challenge is too low, boredom threatens; when it is too high, anxiety or frustration takes over. Keeping the activity within this shifting channel can make it an [[Autotelic Experience]] and sustain [[Engagement]].

Flow requires goals that can be acted on, feedback that supports adjustment, and demands that change as mastery grows. The ideal channel is only one possible shape of play: some games begin in frustration and let practice close the gap, while others pursue reflection or understanding rather than an uninterrupted flow state.

The same challenge-skill relationship can support creative work: excessive demand produces stress, insufficient demand produces boredom, and a demanding but attainable goal enables concentrated, productive absorption.

12282.title: Floating-Point Representation
12282.heading: Floating-Point Representation
12282.content:
Floating-point representation stores a real number using a sign, a finite-precision mantissa, a base, and an integer exponent. It covers a wide range of magnitudes but only a finite set of values.

Numbers that cannot be represented exactly must be rounded or chopped. The resulting [[Round-Off Error]] influences numerical algorithms, especially repeated arithmetic and ill-conditioned problems.

12285.title: Flow-Balance Equations in Queueing
12285.heading: Flow-Balance Equations in Queueing
12285.content:
Flow-balance equations express that, in steady state, the total probability flow into a queueing state equals the total flow out. They relate the long-run proportion of time spent in neighboring occupancy states.

Solving and normalizing these equations yields state probabilities. Operational measures such as blocking probability can then be derived from the probability of the capacity state.

12288.title: Floating-Point Exponent
12288.heading: Floating-Point Exponent
12288.content:
The floating-point exponent scales the mantissa by a power of the representation base. Its range determines the smallest and largest magnitudes the system can encode.

Exponent limits concern range rather than precision: too large a result overflows, while an extremely small result may underflow. The [[Mantissa]] determines how closely values within that range can be represented.
